title: Cache with TTL and Versioned Expiry: implement `put(key, value, ttl, now)` and `get(key, now)` where an entry is valid only while `now < expires_at`; a newer write replaces the old value AND expiry, so an old cleanup event must NOT delete a newer version of the same key (attach a version/sequence to each expiry record and verify it still matches before deleting): lazy expiry gives O(1) per op; a heap for proactive cleanup adds O(log n) and stale-record management.
shortTitle: Cache with TTL and Versioned Expiry
keyPoints: Each entry stores a value, an absolute expiry timestamp (now + ttl), and a version number incremented on every write.
get(key, now) returns the value only if now < expires_at; otherwise reports a miss (lazy expiry).
put(key, value, ttl, now) replaces both the value and the expiry, and bumps the version.
Proactive cleanup uses a min-heap of expiry records, each stamped with the version they were created with.
A cleanup event deletes the entry only if its version matches the record's version; otherwise the record is stale and discarded.
Lazy expiry gives O(1) per get and put; the heap adds O(log n) per put and pop for proactive cleanup.

s1_definition.oneliner: Validate on read against the expiry, and stamp every expiry record with a version so a late cleanup never deletes a newer rewrite.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **TTL cache** – stores each key with an expiry timestamp computed as `now + ttl`; a read is valid only while `now < expires_at`.
- **Versioned expiry** – each write increments a version; cleanup records carry the version they were created with.
- **Lazy expiry** – on `get`, check the timestamp and treat expired entries as misses. O(1) per operation.
- **Proactive cleanup** – a min-heap keyed on expiry time pops expired records; only delete if version matches. O(log n) per push/pop.
- **Stale-record safety** – a late cleanup event with a mismatched version is discarded, protecting freshly rewritten entries.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh's OTP is cached with a two-minute validity. If he requests a new OTP before the old one expires, the new one replaces the old value and its expiry. A background cleanup robot holding a note that says 'delete Rajesh's OTP at 10:02' must check the version number: by then Rajesh has a fresh OTP valid until 10:05, so the robot discards the stale note.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Timeline for key "rajesh-otp":

  Time 100: put("rajesh-otp", "1234", ttl=120)
    Entry: value="1234", expires=220, version=1
    Heap record: (key="rajesh-otp", expires=220, version=1)

  Time 150: put("rajesh-otp", "5678", ttl=120)
    Entry: value="5678", expires=270, version=2
    Heap record: (key="rajesh-otp", expires=270, version=2)

  Time 220: cleanup fires
    Pop record: (expires=220, version=1)
    Current entry version=2 ≠ 1 → STALE → discard
    Entry "5678" survives!

  Time 270: cleanup fires
    Pop record: (expires=270, version=2)
    Current entry version=2 == 2 → DELETE

┌──────────────┬────────┬──────────┬─────────┐
│ Time         │ Action │ Version  │ Entry   │
├──────────────┼────────┼──────────┼─────────┤
│ 100          │ put    │ v1       │ "1234"  │
│ 150          │ put    │ v2       │ "5678"  │
│ 220 (stale)  │ skip   │ v1 ≠ v2 │ "5678"  │
│ 270          │ delete │ v2 == v2 │ removed │
└──────────────┴────────┴──────────┴─────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A cache with time-to-live stores each key alongside an absolute expiry timestamp, and a read is valid only while the current time is strictly before that expiry. Lazy expiry checks validity on every get in O(1), treating expired entries as misses. This is simple but lets expired entries linger in memory.

The subtle correctness problem appears with proactive cleanup. When a key is rewritten with a new value and expiry, a pending cleanup event for the old expiry could fire and delete the fresh entry. The solution is versioning: each write bumps a version number, and each heap record carries the version it was created with. Cleanup only deletes when versions match; otherwise the record is stale and discarded.

The heap adds O(log n) per put and per pop. The lazy get path stays O(1). The strictly-less-than validity comparison must be consistent in both the get and cleanup paths to avoid edge-case inconsistencies.

At the National Bank of India, we cached short-lived transfer authorization codes. Customers frequently refreshed a code before the old one expired. The versioned expiry records ensured background cleanup never deleted a freshly renewed code.

Remember one sentence: stamp every expiry record with a version, and only delete on cleanup if the version still matches the live entry.
